Jacobi, LAPACK dsyevd, Lanczos top-k eigensolvers, and SVD.

#include <iostream>
#include <numerics.hpp>

int main() {
    using namespace num;

    mat A(3, 3, 0.0);
    A(0, 0) = 2.0;
    A(0, 1) = -1.0;
    A(0, 2) = 0.0;
    A(1, 0) = -1.0;
    A(1, 1) = 2.0;
    A(1, 2) = -1.0;
    A(2, 0) = 0.0;
    A(2, 1) = -1.0;
    A(2, 2) = 2.0;

    // 1. Full Symmetric Eigendecomposition
    auto eig_res = lapack::eig_sym(A);
    std::cout << "Eigenvalues: [" << eig_res.values[0] << ", " << eig_res.values[1] << ", "
              << eig_res.values[2] << "]\n";

    // 2. SVD
    auto svd_res = lapack::svd(A);
    std::cout << "Singular Values: [" << svd_res.S[0] << ", " << svd_res.S[1] << ", "
              << svd_res.S[2] << "]\n";

    // Plot spectrum with high-res ASCII dimensions (140 cols x 35 rows)
    std::vector<double> mode_idx{1.0, 2.0, 3.0};
    std::vector<double> eigs{eig_res.values[0], eig_res.values[1], eig_res.values[2]};
    std::vector<double> svs{svd_res.S[0], svd_res.S[1], svd_res.S[2]};

    plt::plot(mode_idx, eigs, "Eigenvalues lambda_k", "linespoints");
    plt::plot(mode_idx, svs, "Singular Values sigma_k", "linespoints");
    plt::title("04 Eigensolvers & SVD: Spectral Spectrum Comparison");
    plt::xlabel("Mode Index k");
    plt::ylabel("Spectral Magnitude");
    plt::legend();
    plt::show_dumb(140, 35);

    return 0;
}

RK4, Adaptive RK45, Verlet, and Yoshida 4th-Order Symplectic Integrators.

#include <iostream>
#include <numerics.hpp>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    using namespace num;

    auto accel = [](const vec &q, vec &a) { a[0] = -q[0]; };

    vec q0{1.0}, v0{0.0};
    ode_params p;
    p.t0 = 0.0;
    p.tf = 10.0;
    p.h = 0.05;

    std::vector<double> t_vec, q_vec, v_vec;
    auto yoshida_stepper = yoshida4(accel, q0, v0, p);
    for (const auto &step : yoshida_stepper) {
        t_vec.push_back(step.t);
        q_vec.push_back(step.q[0]);
        v_vec.push_back(step.v[0]);
    }

    std::cout << "Yoshida 4th-Order Symplectic Integration completed in " << t_vec.size()
              << " steps.\n";

    plt::plot(t_vec, q_vec, "Position q(t)", "lines");
    plt::plot(t_vec, v_vec, "Velocity v(t)", "lines");
    plt::title("05 Symplectic ODE: Yoshida 4th-Order Harmonic Oscillator");
    plt::xlabel("Time t");
    plt::ylabel("Phase Coordinates");
    plt::legend();
    plt::show_dumb(140, 35);

    return 0;
}

docs.title: 06_pde_poisson_solver.cpp
docs.text:
2D/3D scalar/vec Fields & Manufactured Poisson PDE Solvers.

#include <algorithm>
#include <cmath>
#include <iostream>
#include <numerics.hpp>

int main() {
    using namespace num;

    const idx nx = 16, ny = 16, nz = 16;
    const real dx = 1.0 / (nx - 1), dy = 1.0 / (ny - 1), dz = 1.0 / (nz - 1);

    // This mode vanishes on every boundary face.
    scalar_field_3d exact(nx, ny, nz, dx, dy, dz);
    for (idx i = 0; i < nx; ++i) {
        for (idx j = 0; j < ny; ++j) {
            for (idx k = 0; k < nz; ++k) {
                exact(i, j, k) =
                    std::sin(M_PI * i * dx) * std::sin(M_PI * j * dy) * std::sin(M_PI * k * dz);
            }
        }
    }

    // Apply the discrete Laplacian to manufacture a grid-exact source.
    scalar_field_3d source(nx, ny, nz, dx, dy, dz);
    for (idx i = 1; i < nx - 1; ++i) {
        for (idx j = 1; j < ny - 1; ++j) {
            for (idx k = 1; k < nz - 1; ++k) {
                source(i, j, k) = (exact(i + 1, j, k) + exact(i - 1, j, k) + exact(i, j + 1, k) +
                                   exact(i, j - 1, k) + exact(i, j, k + 1) + exact(i, j, k - 1) -
                                   6.0 * exact(i, j, k)) /
                                  (dx * dx);
            }
        }
    }

    scalar_field_3d phi(nx, ny, nz, dx, dy, dz);
    const solver_result result = field_solver::solve_poisson(phi, source, 1e-10, 500);

    real max_error = 0.0;
    for (idx state = 0; state < phi.size(); ++state) {
        max_error = std::max(max_error, std::abs(phi.as_vec()[state] - exact.as_vec()[state]));
    }

    // Extract 1D middle slice phi(x, ny/2, nz/2)
    std::vector<double> x_grid, phi_slice;
    for (idx i = 0; i < nx; ++i) {
        x_grid.push_back((i + 1) * dx);
        phi_slice.push_back(phi(i, ny / 2, nz / 2));
    }

    std::cout << "Poisson converged: " << std::boolalpha << result.converged
              << ", max error = " << max_error << '\n';

    plt::plot(x_grid, phi_slice, "phi(x, y_mid, z_mid)", "lines");
    plt::title("06 PDE field Solver: 1D Mid-Slice Potential Phi(x)");
    plt::xlabel("Position x");
    plt::ylabel("Potential Phi");
    plt::show_dumb(140, 35);

    return result.converged && max_error < 1e-6 ? 0 : 1;
}

docs.title: 07_spectral_fft_transforms.cpp
docs.text:
1D/2D FFT, iFFT, Real rFFT/irfft, and Precomputed fft_plan.

#include <cmath>
#include <iostream>
#include <numerics.hpp>

int main() {
    using namespace num;
    using namespace num::spectral;

    idx n = 64;
    vec r_in(n, 0.0);
    std::vector<double> t_grid(n);
    for (idx i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        t_grid[i] = (2.0 * M_PI / n) * i;
        r_in[i] = std::sin(3.0 * t_grid[i]) + (0.5 * std::cos(7.0 * t_grid[i]));
    }

    cvec r_out((n / 2) + 1, cplx{0, 0});
    rfft(r_in, r_out, fft_backend::seq);

    std::vector<double> k_freq((n / 2) + 1), mag_spec((n / 2) + 1);
    for (idx k = 0; k < (n / 2) + 1; ++k) {
        k_freq[k] = static_cast<double>(k);
        mag_spec[k] = std::abs(r_out[k]);
    }

    std::cout << "rFFT Real Signal transformed into " << mag_spec.size() << " frequency bins.\n";

    plt::plot(t_grid, r_in, "Signal r_in(t)", "lines");
    plt::title("07 Spectral FFT: Input Dual-Frequency Signal");
    plt::xlabel("Time t");
    plt::ylabel("Amplitude");
    plt::show_dumb(140, 30);

    plt::plot(k_freq, mag_spec, "Spectrum |X(k)|", "linespoints");
    plt::title("07 Spectral FFT: Frequency Spectrum Magnitude");
    plt::xlabel("Frequency Bin k");
    plt::ylabel("|X(k)|");
    plt::show_dumb(140, 30);

    return 0;
}

Newton-Raphson, Bisection, Gauss-Legendre & Adaptive Simpson Integration.

#include <cmath>
#include <iostream>
#include <numerics.hpp>

int main() {
    using namespace num;

    // 1. Root Finding: f(x) = x^2 - 2.0 = 0 -> sqrt(2)
    auto f = [](real x) { return (x * x) - 2.0; };
    auto df = [](real x) { return 2.0 * x; };

    auto root_newton = newton(f, df, 1.0, 1e-10, 100);
    auto root_bisect = bisection(f, 1.0, 2.0, 1e-10, 100);
    std::cout << "Newton Root: " << root_newton.root << " | Bisection Root: " << root_bisect.root
              << "\n";

    // Plot target function f(x) over [0, 2]
    std::vector<double> x_val, f_val;
    for (int i = 0; i <= 40; ++i) {
        double x = i * 0.05;
        x_val.push_back(x);
        f_val.push_back(f(x));
    }

    plt::plot(x_val, f_val, "f(x) = x^2 - 2", "lines");
    plt::title("08 Root Finding: Function Curve f(x) with Root at sqrt(2)");
    plt::xlabel("x");
    plt::ylabel("f(x)");
    plt::show_dumb(140, 35);

    return 0;
}

docs.title: 09_mcmc_bayesian_sampling.cpp
docs.text:
Online Running Statistics, Histograms, and Autocorrelation Times.

#include <iostream>
#include <numerics.hpp>
#include <random>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    using namespace num;

    running_stats stats;
    std::mt19937 rng(42);
    std::normal_distribution<double> norm_dist(0.0, 1.0);

    histogram hist(20, -3.0, 3.0);
    for (int i = 0; i < 10000; ++i) {
        double val = norm_dist(rng);
        stats.update(val);
        hist.fill(val);
    }
    std::cout << "Online Welford Mean = " << stats.mean
              << " (Target: 0.0), Variance = " << stats.variance() << " (Target: 1.0)\n";

    // Extract PDF and plot histogram
    auto pdf = hist.pdf();
    std::vector<double> bin_centers, pdf_vals;
    for (idx b = 0; b < hist.nbins; ++b) {
        bin_centers.push_back(hist.bin_centre(b));
        pdf_vals.push_back(pdf[b]);
    }

    plt::plot(bin_centers, pdf_vals, "Sample PDF", "linespoints");
    plt::title("09 Statistics: Sample Probability Density Function (PDF)");
    plt::xlabel("Sample Value x");
    plt::ylabel("Probability Density P(x)");
    plt::show_dumb(140, 35);

    return 0;
}

docs.text:
banded mat storage (KL, KU), banded solves, and compile-time SPD operator tags.

#include <iostream>
#include <numerics.hpp>

int main() {
    using namespace num;

    idx n = 10;
    idx kl = 1, ku = 1;
    band_mat B(n, kl, ku);

    for (idx i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        B(i, i) = 4.0;
        if (i > 0) {
            B(i, i - 1) = -1.0;
        }
        if (i + 1 < n) {
            B(i, i + 1) = -1.0;
        }
    }

    vec b(n, 1.0);
    vec x_sol(n, 0.0);
    banded_solve(B, b, x_sol);

    std::cout << "banded mat (n=" << n << ", kl=" << kl << ", ku=" << ku
              << ") Solved x[0] = " << x_sol[0] << "\n";

    std::vector<double> grid, sol;
    for (idx i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        grid.push_back(static_cast<double>(i));
        sol.push_back(x_sol[i]);
    }

    plt::plot(grid, sol, "banded x", "linespoints");
    plt::title("10 banded Matrices: Solution vec x");
    plt::xlabel("Grid Index i");

docs.title: 12_hessenberg_resolvent_benchmark.cpp
docs.text:
Benchmark comparing naive O(kn^3) full LU batch resolvent against O(n^3 + kn^2) Hessenberg resolvent.

#include <chrono>
#include <cmath>
#include <complex>
#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>
#include <random>
#include <vector>
#include <numerics.hpp>

int main() {
    std::cout << "========================================================================\n";
    std::cout << "  NUMERICS RESOLVENT BENCHMARK: Naive O(k*N^3) LU vs O(N^3 + k*N^2) Hessenberg\n";
    std::cout << "========================================================================\n\n";

    const std::vector<num::idx> sizes = {50, 100, 200, 400};
    const std::size_t num_shifts = 100;

    std::mt19937_64 rng(42);
    std::uniform_real_distribution<double> dist(-1.0, 1.0);

    // Generate 100 sample shifts along the imaginary axis (typical in transfer function & AAA sampling)
    std::vector<num::cplx> shifts(num_shifts);
    for (std::size_t k = 0; k < num_shifts; ++k) {
        shifts[k] = num::cplx(0.1, static_cast<double>(k) * 0.1);
    }

    std::cout << std::left << std::setw(8) << "N"
              << std::setw(10) << "Shifts"
              << std::setw(18) << "Naive LU (ms)"
              << std::setw(20) << "Hessenberg (ms)"
              << std::setw(12) << "Speedup"
              << std::setw(15) << "Max Diff" << "\n";
    std::cout << std::string(80, '-') << "\n";

    for (num::idx n : sizes) {
        num::mat A(n, n, 0.0);
        for (num::idx i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
            for (num::idx j = 0; j < n; ++j) {
                A(i, j) = dist(rng);
            }
            A(i, i) += 5.0; // Ensure well-conditioned
        }

        num::vec b(n);
        for (num::idx i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
            b[i] = dist(rng);
        }

        // 1. Naive O(k * n^3) approach: factorize sI - A fresh on every shift
        auto t0 = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();
        std::vector<std::vector<num::cplx>> naive_sol(num_shifts);
        for (std::size_t k = 0; k < num_shifts; ++k) {
            num::dense_resolvent_solver naive_solver(A);
            naive_solver.factorize(shifts[k]);
            std::vector<num::cplx> b_cplx(n);
            for (num::idx i = 0; i < n; ++i) b_cplx[i] = b[i];
            naive_sol[k] = naive_solver.solve(b_cplx);
        }
        auto t1 = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();
        double naive_ms = std::chrono::duration<double, std::milli>(t1 - t0).count();

        // 2. Optimized O(n^3 + k * n^2) Hessenberg approach
        auto t2 = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();
        num::hessenberg_resolvent_solver hess_solver(A);
        auto hess_sol = hess_solver.solve_batch(shifts, b);
        auto t3 = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();
        double hess_ms = std::chrono::duration<double, std::milli>(t3 - t2).count();

        // Check error agreement
        double max_diff = 0.0;
        for (std::size_t k = 0; k < num_shifts; ++k) {
            for (num::idx i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
                double diff = std::abs(naive_sol[k][i] - hess_sol[k][i]);
                if (diff > max_diff) max_diff = diff;
            }
        }

        double speedup = naive_ms / hess_ms;

        std::cout << std::left << std::setw(8) << n
                  << std::setw(10) << num_shifts
                  << std::setw(18) << std::fixed << std::setprecision(2) << naive_ms
                  << std::setw(20) << std::fixed << std::setprecision(2) << hess_ms
                  << std::setw(12) << std::fixed << std::setprecision(1) << (std::to_string(speedup) + "x")
                  << std::setw(15) << std::scientific << std::setprecision(2) << max_diff << "\n";
    }

    std::cout << "\n========================================================================\n";
    return 0;
}

docs.title: 13_talbot_spectral_validation.cpp
docs.text:
High-precision validation of Talbot contour inversion against Krylov Arnoldi expv using num:: toolkit.

#include <chrono>
#include <cmath>
#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>
#include <random>
#include <vector>
#include <numerics.hpp>

int main() {
    using namespace num;

    std::cout << "========================================================================\n";
    std::cout << "  NUMERICS: TALBOT CONTOUR VS KRYLOV ARNOILDI EXPV VALIDATION\n";
    std::cout << "========================================================================\n\n";

    const idx N = 100;
    std::mt19937_64 rng(42);
    std::uniform_real_distribution<double> weight_dist(0.5, 2.5);
    std::uniform_real_distribution<double> prob_dist(0.0, 1.0);

    // 1. Construct a connected Markov jump generator Q with row sums = 0
    mat Q(N, N, 0.0);
    for (idx i = 0; i < N; ++i) {
        for (idx j = i + 1; j < N; ++j) {
            if (prob_dist(rng) < 0.10 || j == i + 1) { // ensure connected chain
                double rate_ij = weight_dist(rng);
                double rate_ji = weight_dist(rng);
                Q(i, j) = rate_ij;
                Q(j, i) = rate_ji;
            }
        }
    }
    for (idx j = 0; j < N; ++j) {
        double col_rate = 0.0;
        for (idx i = 0; i < N; ++i) {
            if (i != j) col_rate += Q(i, j);
        }
        Q(j, j) = -col_rate;
    }

    vec p0(N, 0.0);
    p0[0] = 1.0; // Initial state at node 0

    // 2. Precompute Hessenberg decomposition of Q once in O(N^3)
    hessenberg_resolvent_solver hess_solver(Q);

    const double t_eval = 1.0;
    std::cout << "Evaluating Markov diffusion at t = " << t_eval << " (N = " << N << " states)...\n";

    // 3. High-precision Ground Truth via Krylov Arnoldi expv
    operators::dense_op Q_op(Q);
    auto t_krylov_start = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();
    vec p_exact = expv(t_eval, Q_op, p0, 50, 1e-15);
    auto t_krylov_end = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();
    double krylov_ms = std::chrono::duration<double, std::milli>(t_krylov_end - t_krylov_start).count();

    std::cout << "Krylov-Arnoldi ground truth computed in " << std::fixed << std::setprecision(2) << krylov_ms << " ms.\n\n";

    // 4. Parameter sweep over Talbot quadrature modes M
    const std::vector<idx> modes = {4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 20, 24, 28, 32};
    std::vector<double> modes_dbl, err_inf_list, err_l1_list;

    std::cout << std::left << std::setw(12) << "Nodes (M)"
              << std::setw(18) << "Walltime (ms)"
              << std::setw(18) << "L_inf Error"
              << std::setw(18) << "L_1 Error" << "\n";
    std::cout << std::string(66, '-') << "\n";

    for (idx M : modes) {
        auto t0 = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();
        std::vector<cplx> density(N, cplx(0.0, 0.0));

        for (const auto &[shift, weight] : talbot_contour(t_eval, M)) {
            auto sol = hess_solver.solve(shift, p0);
            for (idx i = 0; i < N; ++i) {
                density[i] += weight * sol[i];
            }
        }

        vec p_talbot(N, 0.0);
        for (idx i = 0; i < N; ++i) p_talbot[i] = std::max(0.0, density[i].real());
        clip_and_normalize_nonnegative(p_talbot);

        auto t1 = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();
        double ms = std::chrono::duration<double, std::milli>(t1 - t0).count();

        double l_inf = 0.0, l_1 = 0.0;
        for (idx i = 0; i < N; ++i) {
            double diff = std::abs(p_talbot[i] - p_exact[i]);
            l_inf = std::max(l_inf, diff);
            l_1 += diff;
        }

        modes_dbl.push_back(static_cast<double>(M));
        err_inf_list.push_back(std::max(1e-16, l_inf));
        err_l1_list.push_back(std::max(1e-16, l_1));

        std::cout << std::left << std::setw(12) << M
                  << std::setw(18) << std::fixed << std::setprecision(3) << ms
                  << std::setw(18) << std::scientific << std::setprecision(3) << l_inf
                  << std::setw(18) << std::scientific << std::setprecision(3) << l_1 << "\n";
    }

    // 5. Multi-panel Visualization
    std::cout << "\nRendering ASCII convergence profile...\n";
    plt::plot(modes_dbl, err_inf_list, "L_inf Error", "linespoints");
    plt::plot(modes_dbl, err_l1_list, "L_1 Error", "linespoints");
    plt::title("13 Talbot Spectral Convergence vs Modes M (t = 1.0)");
    plt::xlabel("Talbot Quadrature Nodes M");
    plt::ylabel("Absolute Error vs Arnoldi expv");
    plt::semilogy();
    plt::legend();
    plt::show_dumb(120, 25);

    plt::savefig("13_talbot_spectral_validation.png");
    std::cout << "\nSaved high-resolution plot to 13_talbot_spectral_validation.png\n";
    std::cout << "========================================================================\n";

    return 0;
}

docs.title: 14_concepts_and_property_invariants.cpp
docs.text:
Demonstrates C++20 linear algebra concepts, compile-time invariant tagging (assume_spd), and loud warnings on untagged storage.

#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>
#include <numerics.hpp>

int main() {
    using namespace num;

    std::cout << "========================================================================\n";
    std::cout << "  14: C++20 Linear Algebra Invariants & Loud Diagnostics Demonstration  \n";
    std::cout << "========================================================================\n\n";

    // -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    // 1. Construct a 4x4 Symmetric Positive-Definite (SPD) 1D Laplace mat
    // -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    mat A(4, 4, 0.0);
    A(0, 0) = 2.0; A(0, 1) = -1.0;
    A(1, 0) = -1.0; A(1, 1) = 2.0; A(1, 2) = -1.0;
    A(2, 1) = -1.0; A(2, 2) = 2.0; A(2, 3) = -1.0;
    A(3, 2) = -1.0; A(3, 3) = 2.0;

    vec b{1.0, 2.0, 2.0, 1.0};

    // -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    // 2. Untagged input does not compile; the escape hatch is explicit
    // -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    std::cout << "--- [Case 1: Deliberate opt-out via num::unsafe::cholesky(A)] ---\n";
    std::cout << "cholesky(assume_spd(A)) on a raw mat is a compile error: a raw matrix carries no SPD\n"
                 "invariant, and Cholesky is undefined without one. Uncommenting the line below\n"
                 "fails to build, rather than warning and continuing:\n\n"
                 "    // auto bad = cholesky(assume_spd(A));  // error: static assertion failed\n\n"
                 "To take the precondition on faith anyway, say so at the call site:\n";

    auto chol_untagged = unsafe::cholesky(A); // opt-out, greppable, no verification
    vec x_untagged(4, 0.0);
    cholesky_solve(chol_untagged, b, x_untagged);
    std::cout << "unsafe:: Solution x = [" << x_untagged[0] << ", " << x_untagged[1] << ", "
              << x_untagged[2] << ", " << x_untagged[3] << "]\n\n";

    // -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    // 3. Demonstration of Tagged Input via assume_spd(A) -> 100% Warning-Free
    // -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    std::cout << "--- [Case 2: Tagged Invariant Input cholesky(assume_spd(A))] ---\n";
    std::cout << "Wrapping with assume_spd(A) makes it an spd_operator and runs 100% warning-free:\n";

    auto spd_matrix = assume_spd(A);

    // Static concept verification at compile time:
    static_assert(spd_operator<decltype(spd_matrix)>, "assume_spd attaches law::spd");
    static_assert(self_adjoint_operator<decltype(spd_matrix)>, "spd implies self-adjoint");

    auto chol_tagged = cholesky(spd_matrix);
    vec x_tagged(4, 0.0);
    cholesky_solve(chol_tagged, b, x_tagged);
    std::cout << "Tagged Solution x   = [" << x_tagged[0] << ", " << x_tagged[1] << ", "
              << x_tagged[2] << ", " << x_tagged[3] << "]\n\n";

    // -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    // 4. Demonstration of Dynamic Invariant Validation via make_spd(A)
    // -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    std::cout << "--- [Case 3: Dynamic Validation via make_spd(A)] ---\n";
    try {
        auto validated = make_spd(A);
        std::cout << "make_spd(A) successfully validated positive definiteness.\n";
    } catch (const std::exception &e) {
        std::cout << "Validation error: " << e.what() << "\n";
    }

    mat Indefinite(2, 2, 0.0);
    Indefinite(0, 0) = 1.0; Indefinite(0, 1) = 3.0;
    Indefinite(1, 0) = 3.0; Indefinite(1, 1) = 1.0; // det = -8 < 0
    std::cout << "Testing make_spd on Indefinite mat [[1, 3], [3, 1]]...\n";
    try {
        auto invalid = make_spd(Indefinite);
        (void)invalid;
    } catch (const std::exception &e) {
        std::cout << "[Caught Expected Violation] " << e.what() << "\n\n";
    }

    // -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    // 5. In-Terminal Solution Visualization
    // -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    std::vector<double> grid{0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0};
    std::vector<double> sol{x_tagged[0], x_tagged[1], x_tagged[2], x_tagged[3]};

    plt::plot(grid, sol, "x_solution", "linespoints");
    plt::title("14 Concepts & Property Invariants: 1D Poisson Solution");
    plt::xlabel("Grid Node i");
    plt::ylabel("Solution x_i");
    plt::show_dumb(120, 25);

    std::cout << "\n[SUCCESS] Example 14 completed.\n";
    return 0;
}

docs.title: 15_diffusion_evidence_cg.cpp
docs.text:
End-to-end invariant propagation from a PDE construction into CG.

#include "numerics.hpp"

#include <cmath>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    constexpr int points_per_side = 32;
    constexpr double timestep_diffusivity = 0.05;

    const num::grid2d grid{points_per_side, 1.0 / (points_per_side + 1)};

    // The Dirichlet backward-Euler construction establishes that I - dt*L is
    // positive definite.  That evidence is part of the returned operator, so
    // CG accepts it directly: there is no assume_spd() at the call site.
    const num::operators::backward_euler_2d system(grid.N, timestep_diffusivity);
    static_assert(num::claims<decltype(system), num::law::spd>);

    num::vec rhs(grid.size(), 0.0);
    for (int i = 0; i < grid.N; ++i) {
        for (int j = 0; j < grid.N; ++j) {
            const double x = grid.x(i);
            const double y = grid.y(j);
            rhs[grid.flat(i, j)] = std::sin(num::pi * x) * std::sin(num::pi * y);
        }
    }

    num::vec solution(rhs.size(), 0.0);
    const auto result =
        num::cg(system, rhs, solution,
                num::cg_options{.tolerance = 1e-12, .max_iterations = 4 * solution.size()});

    std::cout << "backward-Euler diffusion: " << result.iterations << " CG iterations, residual "
              << result.residual << '\n';
    return result.converged ? 0 : 1;
}

Defined in header <roots/roots.hpp>

template <typename Float = double, std::invocable<Float> Func = scalar_fn>
basic_root_result<Float> bisection(Func &&f, Float a, Float b, Float tol = Float{1e-10},
                                   idx max_iter = 1000);

Bisection method for finding a root on a bracketing interval \([a, b]\) where \(f(a) f(b) \le 0\).

Guaranteed linear convergence halving the interval width at each step: \(|x_k - x^*| \le \frac{b-a}{2^k}\).

docs.title: num::bracketable_function
docs.text:
Defined in header <roots/concepts.hpp>

template <class F, class T = real>
concept bracketable_function = scalar_function<F, T> && std::totally_ordered<T>;

Function whose sign can be compared across an interval.

\[ f(a) \, f(b) < 0 \]

A sign change guarantees a root by the intermediate value theorem, which is what makes bisection and Brent's method unconditionally convergent. Whether a given \([a,b]\) brackets a root depends on the values, so it is checked by num::roots::debug::verify_bracket.

Defined in header <linear/factorization/cholesky.hpp>, <linear/factorization/factor.hpp>

cholesky_result cholesky(const with_law<mat, law::spd> &A);  // (1)

template <class M>
requires matrix_space<M> && (!claims<M, law::spd>)

similar_factor<cholesky_result> cholesky(const spmat &R, view<const real> h);  // (3)

similar_factor<block_cholesky_factor>
cholesky(const spmat &R, block_structure structure, view<const real> h);  // (4)

(1) Factor a matrix whose SPD property has already been established.

(2) Rejects an untagged matrix at compile time.

Cholesky is defined only for symmetric positive definite matrices, so a raw mat does not satisfy its precondition. This overload exists to say so in a diagnostic rather than to run: a warning can be silenced by an unrelated -Wno- flag, whereas this cannot compile.

(3) Factor H R H^-1 by Cholesky and retain H for applications of R^-1.

(4) Block-Cholesky specialization of the diagonally similar factorization.

docs.title: num::gaussian_probe
docs.text:
Defined in header <stochastic/probe.hpp>

template <typename RNG = rng>
mat gaussian_probe(idx n, idx probes, RNG &generator);  // (1)

mat gaussian_probe(idx n, idx probes, unsigned seed);  // (2)

(1) An \(n \times p\) matrix of independent standard Gaussian probes.

Like rademacher_probe, column \(k\) satisfies \(E[z_k z_k^T] = I\), so either family drives a Hutchinson estimator. Gaussian probes are the ones to reach for when the estimator's concentration is stated through a chi-square tail bound, since each row of the probed block is then exactly chi-square.

(2) The same Gaussian probe from a fixed seed.

docs.title: num::gmres
docs.text:
Defined in header <linear/solvers/gmres.hpp>

template <class Op, class V>
requires math::inner_product_space<V> && math::linear_operator<Op, V, V> &&
         std::same_as<math::scalar_t<V>, real>
solver_result gmres(const Op &A, const V &b, V &x, gmres_options options = {});  // (1)

template <class Op, class M, class V>
requires math::inner_product_space<V> && math::linear_operator<Op, V, V> &&
         math::linear_operator<M, V, V> && std::floating_point<math::scalar_t<V>>
solver_result gmres(const Op &A, const M &preconditioner, const V &b, V &x,
                    gmres_options options = {});  // (2)

solver_result gmres(const spmat &A, const vec &b, vec &x, gmres_options options = {});  // (3)

solver_result gmres(const mat &A, const vec &b, vec &x, gmres_options options = {});  // (4)

(1) Solve general unsymmetric linear systems \(A x = b\) using restarted GMRES.

Constructs an orthogonal Arnoldi basis \(V_m\) and solves the projected least-squares problem \(\min \| \beta e_1 - \bar{H}_m y \|_2\) with Givens plane rotations.

(2) Right-preconditioned restarted GMRES: solves \(A M^{-1} u = b\), \(x = M^{-1} u\).

Right preconditioning keeps result.residual equal to \(\|b - Ax\|_2\), so the stopping test does not depend on the scaling of M. M need not be symmetric, as with ILU(0).

(3) Solve sparse linear systems \(A x = b\) using restarted GMRES.

(4) Solve dense linear systems \(A x = b\) using restarted GMRES with hardware backend dispatch.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• A: General square linear operator (dense, sparse, or matrix-free).
  • b: Right-hand side vector.
  • x: Solution vector (serves as initial guess on input, updated in place).
  • options: Tolerance on \(\|b - A x\|_2\), iteration limit, and restart length.
  • preconditioner: Approximate inverse applied on the right.

docs.title: Return value
docs.text: solver_result containing iteration count, final residual norm, and convergence boolean.

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text: • std::invalid_argument: If dimensions do not match.

docs.title: See also
docs.text: cg, minres, pcg

docs.title: num::graph_distance_levels
docs.text:
Defined in header <linear/graph/levels.hpp>

array<idx> graph_distance_levels(const spmat &A, view<const idx> seeds);  // (1)

array<idx> graph_distance_levels(const spmat &A, idx seed);  // (2)

(1) Label each row by its graph distance from a seed set.

An edge joins rows whose distances differ by at most one, so grouping by distance makes the matrix block-tridiagonal, as build_block_order and factor_block_lu need. A component no seed reaches restarts at distance zero from its own search. With L balanced levels, elimination costs \(O(n^3/L^2)\).

(2) The same labels from a single seed row.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• A: Square CSR matrix whose undirected support graph is traversed.
  • seeds: Rows at distance zero. Empty means every component starts from its lowest-numbered row.

docs.title: Return value
docs.text: One level label per row.

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text: • std::invalid_argument: If A is not square or a seed is out of range.

docs.title: num::hessenberg_resolvent_solver
docs.text:
Defined in header <linear/solvers/hessenberg_resolvent.hpp>

class hessenberg_resolvent_solver;

High-performance resolvent solver (sI - A)^-1 b reusing a precomputed Hessenberg decomposition.

docs.title: num::hessenberg_shifted_solve
docs.text:
Defined in header <linear/factorization/hessenberg.hpp>

void hessenberg_shifted_solve(const mat &H, cplx shift, const array<cplx> &b_tilde,
                              array<cplx> &y, array<cplx> &M_buf, array<idx> &pivots);

Solve the shifted Hessenberg system \((sI - H)y = \tilde b\) in \(O(n^2)\).

Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting on an upper Hessenberg matrix touches one subdiagonal per column, so the factorization is \(O(n^2)\) rather than \(O(n^3)\). This is what makes a resolvent \((sI-A)^{-1}b\) cheap once \(A\) has been reduced once: every subsequent shift reuses the same \(H\).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• H: Upper Hessenberg matrix, n*n.
  • shift: The scalar s.
  • b_tilde: Right-hand side, length n.
  • y: Output, resized to n.
  • M_buf: Scratch, grown to n*n and reusable across calls.
  • pivots: Scratch, grown to n and reusable across calls.

docs.title: num::inverse_diagonal
docs.text:
Defined in header <linear/factorization/factor.hpp>, <linear/factorization/inverse_diagonal.hpp>, <linear/factorization/probed_inverse_diagonal.hpp>

void inverse_diagonal(const lu_result &factor, vec &result,
                      inverse_diagonal_workspace &workspace, idx block_size = 64);  // (1)

void inverse_diagonal(const cholesky_result &factor, vec &result,
                      inverse_diagonal_workspace &workspace, idx block_size = 64);  // (2)

void inverse_diagonal(const klu_factorization &factor, vec &result,
                      inverse_diagonal_workspace &workspace, idx block_size = 64);  // (3)

void inverse_diagonal(const auto_linear_solver &factor, vec &result,
                      inverse_diagonal_workspace &workspace, idx block_size = 64);  // (4)

vec inverse_diagonal(const auto_linear_solver &factor, idx block_size = 64);  // (5)

template <class F>
vec inverse_diagonal(const F &Z, idx n);  // (6)

template <retained_factorization F>
vec inverse_diagonal(const F &factor, const spmat &matrix,
                     view<const real> symmetrizer = {},
                     inverse_diagonal_options options = {});  // (7)

(1) Compute diag(A^-1) through blocked identity solves.

(2) Compute diag(A^-1) from a Cholesky factor using blocked identity solves.

(3) Compute diag(A^-1) from a KLU factor using blocked identity solves.

(4) Compute diag(A^-1) from an automatically selected reusable factor.

(5) Convenience overload owning its result and workspace.

Allocates; prefer the workspace form in hot loops.

(6) Undocumented.

(7) Estimate \(\operatorname{diag}(A^{-1})\) for a nonsingular M-matrix from one block of Gaussian probes, without one solve per entry.

A diagonal similarity makes the symmetric part positive definite, so each entry is a squared row norm, estimated without bias by the probe mean square. The derivation is in the algorithm notes.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• factor: A retained factorization of matrix.
  • matrix: The nonsingular M-matrix A, in CSR form.
  • symmetrizer: \(\sqrt{\pi}\) when A is similar to a symmetric matrix through \(\operatorname{Diag}(\sqrt{\pi})\), which saves the two scaling solves. Empty otherwise.
  • options: Probe count, Krylov depth, tolerance, and seed.

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text:
• std::invalid_argument: If no probes are requested.
  • std::runtime_error: If matrix is not a nonsingular M-matrix.

docs.title: num::lanczos
docs.text:
Defined in header <linear/eigen/lanczos.hpp>

template <class Op>
requires self_adjoint_operator<Op, vec>
lanczos_result lanczos(const Op &A, idx k, real tol = 1e-10, idx max_steps = 0);  // (1)

lanczos_result lanczos(const with_law<mat, law::self_adjoint> &A, idx k,
                       real tol = 1e-10, idx max_steps = 0);  // (2)

(1) Compute the largest \(k\) extremal Ritz pairs of a symmetric / self-adjoint operator using Lanczos iteration.

Builds an orthonormal Krylov basis with modified Gram-Schmidt reorthogonalization, generates a symmetric tridiagonal projection \(T_m\), and extracts Ritz values and Ritz vectors.

(2) Compute the largest \(k\) Ritz pairs of a matrix claiming law::self_adjoint.

docs.title: Template parameters
docs.text: • Op: Linear operator type satisfying self_adjoint_operator<Op, vec>.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• A: Self-adjoint linear operator (matrix-free callable, sparse, or dense wrapper).
  • k: Number of extremal eigenpairs to compute (\(0 < k \le n\)).
  • tol: Residual tolerance \(\|A v - \lambda v\|_2\) for declaring convergence (default: 1e-10).
  • max_steps: Maximum Lanczos steps to perform (defaults to \(\min(3k, n)\)).

docs.title: Return value
docs.text:
lanczos_result containing Ritz values, column Ritz vectors, steps performed, and convergence flag.

lanczos_result with Ritz pairs and convergence metadata.

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text: • std::invalid_argument: If k is invalid or operator is not square.

docs.title: See also
docs.text: eig_sym, power_iteration

docs.title: num::low_rank_difference
docs.text:
Defined in header <linear/factorization/woodbury.hpp>

low_rank_update low_rank_difference(const spmat &base, const spmat &current,
                                    view<const idx> changed);

Express \(B - A\) as \(PQ^{T}\) when the two differ only in the listed rows and columns.

Changing k indices of a square matrix touches at most k rows and k columns, so the difference has rank at most 2k. The first k columns of P are the corresponding unit vectors and carry the changed rows in Q; the last k columns of Q are the unit vectors and carry the changed columns in P, excluding entries a changed row already accounts for.

docs.title: num::lu
docs.text:
Defined in header <linear/factorization/factor.hpp>, <linear/factorization/lu.hpp>, <linear/factorization/reuse.hpp>

lu_result lu(const mat &A);  // (1)

no_pivot_lu lu(const mat &R, no_pivot_structure);  // (2)

block_lu_factor lu(const spmat &R, block_structure structure);  // (4)

auto_linear_solver lu(const spmat &R, sparse_structure);  // (5)

friend corrected_lu lu(const spmat &R, no_pivot_structure, const corrected_lu *previous,
                       view<const idx> changed);  // (6)

suffix_block_lu lu(const spmat &R, block_structure structure,
                   const suffix_block_lu *previous, view<const idx> changed);  // (7)

(1) Factor \(PA = LU\) with partial pivoting.

Uses LAPACK dgetrf above lapack_factor_threshold when an optimized LAPACK is configured, else the in-tree blocked kernel. Call num::lapack::lu or num::seq::lu to force one.

(2) Factor a dense unstructured nonsingular M-matrix by no-pivot LU.

(3) Factor a sparse unstructured nonsingular M-matrix by no-pivot LU.

(4) Factor a block-tridiagonal nonsingular M-matrix by block LU.

(5) Factor a large unstructured matrix with the configured sparse backend.

(6) No-pivot LU of R, corrected from previous when few slots differ.

(7) Block LU of R, copying the unchanged prefix of previous.

docs.title: num::minres
docs.text:
Defined in header <linear/solvers/minres.hpp>

template <class Op, class V>
requires math::inner_product_space<V> && math::self_adjoint_operator<Op, V> &&
         std::same_as<math::scalar_t<V>, real>
solver_result minres(const Op &A, const V &b, V &x, minres_options options = {});

Solve \(A x = b\) using MINRES (Minimum Residual) for symmetric / self-adjoint systems.

Minimizes the 2-norm of the residual \(\|b - A x_k\|_2\) over the Krylov subspace \(\mathcal{K}_k(A, r_0)\). Unlike CG, MINRES converges stably on symmetric indefinite linear systems.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• A: Symmetric / self-adjoint linear operator (e.g. num::assume_symmetric(A)).
  • b: Right-hand side vector.
  • x: Solution vector (serves as initial guess on input, updated in place).
  • options: Tolerance on \(\|b - A x\|_2\) and iteration limit.

docs.title: Return value
docs.text: solver_result containing iteration count, final residual norm, and convergence boolean.

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text: • std::invalid_argument: If dimensions of A, b, and x do not match.

docs.title: See also
docs.text: cg, gmres, pcg, assume_symmetric

docs.title: num::moment_accumulator
docs.text:
Defined in header <stats/concepts.hpp>

template <class A, class T = real>
concept moment_accumulator = streaming_accumulator<A, T> && requires(const A &acc) {
  { acc.variance() } -> std::convertible_to<T>;
  { acc.std_dev() } -> std::convertible_to<T>;
};

Accumulator reporting the first two moments.

\[ \mu_n = \mu_{n-1} + \frac{x_n - \mu_{n-1}}{n}, \qquad s^2 = \frac{M_{2,n}}{n - 1} \]

The recurrence is used rather than \(\sum x^2 - n\mu^2\) because the latter cancels catastrophically when the variance is small relative to the mean.

docs.title: num::newton
docs.text:
Defined in header <roots/roots.hpp>

template <typename Float = double, std::invocable<Float> Func = scalar_fn,
          std::invocable<Float> DFunc = scalar_fn>
basic_root_result<Float> newton(Func &&f, DFunc &&df, Float x0,
                                Float tol = Float{1e-10}, idx max_iter = 1000);

Newton–Raphson method with quadratic convergence using analytical derivative \(f'(x)\).

Iteratively computes \(x_{k+1} = x_k - \frac{f(x_k)}{f'(x_k)}\). Achieves quadratic convergence \(\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^2)\) near simple roots.

  • max_iter: Maximum iterations (default: 1000).

docs.title: num::pcg
docs.text:
Defined in header <linear/solvers/pcg.hpp>

template <class Op, class M, class V>
requires math::inner_product_space<V> && math::spd_operator<Op, V> &&
         math::spd_operator<M, V> && std::floating_point<math::scalar_t<V>>
solver_result pcg(const Op &A, const M &preconditioner, const V &b, V &x,
                  pcg_options options = {});  // (1)

template <class Subspace, class Op, class M, class V>
requires math::inner_product_space<V> && math::linear_subspace_of<Subspace, V> &&
         math::linear_operator<Op, V, V> && math::linear_operator<M, V, V> &&
         claims<Op, law::spd_on<Subspace>> && claims<M, law::spd_on<Subspace>> &&
         std::floating_point<math::scalar_t<V>>
solver_result pcg(const Op &A, const M &preconditioner, const V &b, V &x,
                  const Subspace &subspace, pcg_options options = {});  // (2)

(1) Solve \(A x = b\) using Preconditioned Conjugate Gradient (PCG).

Accelerates CG convergence using a symmetric positive-definite preconditioner \(M \approx A^{-1}\). Both the system operator A and the preconditioner M must claim law::spd.

(2) PCG on a named invariant subspace.

Evidence for A and M is tied to the exact same Subspace type, and membership is checked throughout the recurrence.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• A: Symmetric positive-definite linear operator or matrix wrapper.
  • preconditioner: preconditioner operator approximating \(A^{-1}\) (e.g. Jacobi, Incomplete Cholesky).
  • b: Right-hand side vector.
  • x: Solution vector (serves as initial guess on input, updated in place).
  • options: Tolerance on the residual norm and iteration limit.

docs.title: Return value
docs.text: solver_result containing iteration count, final residual norm, and convergence boolean.

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text: • std::invalid_argument: If dimensions of A, preconditioner, b, and x do not match.

docs.title: See also
docs.text: cg, minres, gmres, approx_chol_preconditioner

docs.title: num::refactor_block_cholesky_suffix
docs.text:
Defined in header <linear/factorization/block_tridiagonal.hpp>

block_cholesky_factor
refactor_block_cholesky_suffix(const spmat &A, view<const idx> levels,
                               const block_cholesky_factor &previous,
                               idx first_changed_block);

Reuse a block-Cholesky prefix and refactor only the changed suffix.

The retained diagonal factors are 0,...,j-1, and the retained scaled lower blocks are 0,...,j-2, where j = first_changed_block. The boundary coupling j-1 is recomputed because it touches the changed suffix.

docs.title: num::refactor_block_lu_suffix
docs.text:
Defined in header <linear/factorization/block_tridiagonal.hpp>

block_lu_factor refactor_block_lu_suffix(const spmat &A, view<const idx> levels,
                                         const block_lu_factor &previous,
                                         idx first_changed_block, real scale = 1.0);

Reuse a block-LU prefix and refactor only the changed suffix.

Blocks before first_changed_block must be numerically unchanged from the matrix represented by previous. The coupling immediately before the changed block is assembled and eliminated again, because it touches the changed suffix. Thus a change beginning at block j retains diagonal factors 0,...,j-1 and scaled lower blocks 0,...,j-2.

The layout of the retained prefix is checked, while equality of its matrix entries is the caller's responsibility.

docs.title: num::retained_factorization
docs.text:
Defined in header <linear/factorization/woodbury.hpp>

template <class F, class Vec = vec, class Mat = mat> concept retained_factorization = vector_space<Vec> && (requires(const F &factor, const Vec &v, const Mat &m, Vec &vout, Mat &mout) { solve(factor, v, vout); solve(factor, m, mout); solve_transpose(factor, v, vout); solve_transpose(factor, m, mout); } || requires(const F &factor, const Vec &v, const Mat &m, Vec &vout, Mat &mout) { factor.solve(v, vout); factor.solve(m, mout); factor.solve_transpose(v, vout); factor.solve_transpose(m, mout); });

A reusable factorization that applies \(A^{-1}\) and \(A^{-T}\).

Woodbury needs the transpose, which direct_factorization does not promise, and it needs out-of-place solves so a corrected result can be formed without destroying the right-hand side. The out-parameter forms may alias their input.

docs.title: num::secant
docs.text:
Defined in header <roots/roots.hpp>

template <typename Float = double, std::invocable<Float> Func = scalar_fn>
basic_root_result<Float> secant(Func &&f, Float x0, Float x1, Float tol = Float{1e-10},
                                idx max_iter = 1000);

Secant quasi-Newton root-finding method requiring two initial guesses \(x_0, x_1\).

Replaces the exact derivative with a finite difference chord: \(x_{k+1} = x_k - f(x_k) \frac{x_k - x_{k-1}}{f(x_k) - f(x_{k-1})}\). Superlinear convergence order \(\approx 1.618\).

void thomas(const basic_vec<Float> &a, const basic_vec<Float> &b,
            const basic_vec<Float> &c, const basic_vec<Float> &d, basic_vec<Float> &x);

Solve tridiagonal linear system \(a_{i-1} x_{i-1} + b_i x_i + c_i x_{i+1} = d_i\) in \(\mathcal{O}(n)\) time.

template <bool Parallel = false, typename Float = double,
          std::invocable<Float> Func = scalar_fn>
Float trapz(Func &&f, Float a, Float b, idx n = 100);

Composite Trapezoidal numerical integration over \([a, b]\) with \(n\) panels.

Computes \(\int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x \approx h \left( \frac{f(a)+f(b)}{2} + \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} f(a+ih) \right)\) with \(\mathcal{O}(h^2)\) error.

docs.title: num::woodbury_solver
docs.text:
Defined in header <linear/factorization/woodbury.hpp>

template <retained_factorization F>
class woodbury_solver;

Solves with \(A_{base} + PQ^{T}\) through the retained factor of \(A_{base}\).

The Woodbury identity gives \(x = y - WG^{-1}P^{T}y\) with \(y = A_{base}^{-T}b\), \(W = A_{base}^{-T}Q\) and \(G = I + P^{T}W\), and the mirror identity for forward solves. Construction costs one rank-p transpose solve. \(A_{base}^{-1}P\) and \(A_{base}^{-T}W\) are formed on first use, so a caller that only solves transposes never pays for them.

The base factorization is referenced, not copied, and must outlive this object.

docs.title: Members
docs.text: member description woodbury_solver(const F &base, low_rank_update update) idx rank() const The rank p of the update. idx size() const The order n of the corrected matrix. const mat &left() const P. const mat &transpose_right() const \(W = A_{base}^{-T}Q\). const mat &inverse_left() const \(A_{base}^{-1}P\), formed on first use. const mat &transpose_right_squared() const \(A_{base}^{-T}W\), formed on first use. void right_solve(mat &y, vec &scratch) const Replace y by \(yG^{-1}\), solving \(G^{T}y_i^{T} = y_i^{T}\) per row. template <class RightHandSide> RightHandSide solve_transpose(const RightHandSide &rhs) const Solve \((A_{base} + PQ^{T})^{T}x = b\). template <class RightHandSide> RightHandSide solve(const RightHandSide &rhs) const Solve \((A_{base} + PQ^{T})x = b\). vec inverse_diagonal(view<const real> base_diagonal) const \(diag(A_{new}^{-1})\) from the base diagonal. \(diag(A_{new}^{-1}) = diag(A_{base}^{-1}) - diag(A_{base}^{-1}PG^{-1}Q^{T}A_{base}^{-1})\), which costs no solve beyond the two rank-p blocks already held.

docs.title: num::concepts::addressable_priority_queue
docs.text:
Defined in header <structures/concepts.hpp>

template <typename T, typename Key = double, typename Index = num::idx>
concept addressable_priority_queue =
    std::totally_ordered<Key> && requires(T pq, Index index, const Key &key) {
      { pq.push(index, key) } -> std::same_as<void>;
      { pq.pop() } -> std::same_as<void>;
      { pq.top_index() } -> std::same_as<Index>;
      { pq.top_key() } -> std::convertible_to<Key>;
      { pq.contains(index) } -> std::same_as<bool>;
      { pq.update(index, key) } -> std::same_as<void>;
      { pq.empty() } -> std::same_as<bool>;
      { pq.size() } -> std::same_as<Index>;
    };

Totally ordered key set with addressable elements and a retrievable minimum.

top_key() is the minimum over every contained key, maintained across push, pop, and update. update revises a key in place, which is what Dijkstra and Prim need and a plain priority queue cannot do.

docs.title: num::concepts::equivalence_relation
docs.text:
Defined in header <structures/concepts.hpp>

template <typename T, typename Index = num::idx>
concept equivalence_relation = requires(T ds, Index u, Index v) {
  { ds.find(u) } -> std::same_as<Index>;
  { ds.unite(u, v) } -> std::same_as<bool>;
  { ds.connected(u, v) } -> std::same_as<bool>;
  { ds.count() } -> std::same_as<Index>;
  { ds.size() } -> std::same_as<Index>;
};

Equivalence relation \(\sim\) on \(\{0,\dots,N-1\}\) with its quotient set.

find(u) selects the canonical representative of \([u]\) and is therefore idempotent. connected(u,v) decides \(u \sim v\) and must agree with \(\mathrm{find}(u) = \mathrm{find}(v)\). unite(u,v) replaces \(\sim\) by the finest relation containing it in which \(u \sim v\). count() is the size of the quotient and drops by one per successful unite.

docs.title: num::concepts::incidence_structure
docs.text:
Defined in header <structures/concepts.hpp>

template <typename G, typename Index = num::idx>
concept incidence_structure = requires(const G g, Index u) {
  { g.n_vertices() } -> std::same_as<Index>;
  { g.n_edges() } -> std::same_as<Index>;
  { g.degree(u) } -> std::same_as<Index>;
  { g.neighbors(u) };
};

Finite incidence structure \(G = (V, E)\) with \(E \subseteq V \times V\).

neighbors(u) enumerates \(\{v : (u,v) \in E\}\) and degree(u) is that set's cardinality. The two must agree, and for an undirected graph the handshake lemma \(\sum_u \deg(u) = 2|E|\) must hold.

docs.title: num::kernel::gemm
docs.text:
Defined in header <kernel/dense.hpp>

template <std::floating_point T>
void gemm(T *C, idx ldc, const T *A, idx lda, const T *B, idx ldb, T alpha, T beta,
          idx m, idx n, idx k, T *work) noexcept;  // (1)

template <std::floating_point T>
void gemm(T *C, idx ldc, const T *A, idx lda, const T *B, idx ldb, T alpha, T beta,
          idx m, idx n, idx k) noexcept;  // (2)

template <std::floating_point T>
void gemm(T *C, const T *A, const T *B, T alpha, T beta, idx m, idx n, idx k) noexcept;  // (3)

(1) Dense matrix product C <- alpha*A*B + beta*C, with row strides and caller-provided workspace.

A is m x k, B is k x n, C is m x n; work holds at least gemm_workspace<T>(m, n, k) elements. A, B, C and work must not overlap. See gemm_config for the blocking.

(2) Dense matrix product C <- alpha*A*B + beta*C, with row strides.

Packs through a per-thread static buffer (see detail::gemm_scratch); pass a workspace explicitly to keep the call free of any state.

(3) Undocumented.

docs.title: num::kernel::gemm_config
docs.text:
Defined in header <kernel/dense.hpp>

template <std::floating_point T>
struct gemm_config;

The blocking gemm uses on this target, derived at compile time.

The Goto/BLIS structure: an mr x nr register-tiled microkernel over kc inner products, fed from packed panels of A and B. mr and nr come from the vector width and register count, and kc, mc, nc from NUM_K_L1_BYTES, NUM_K_L2_BYTES and NUM_K_GEMM_PANEL_BYTES. See the kernel page for the per-target shapes.

docs.title: Members
docs.text: member description static constexpr idx width = / sizeof(T) Elements per vector register. static constexpr idx b_vectors = (>= 32 && width <= 2) ? 3 : 2 B vectors held per microkernel: three when the file is wide and the vectors narrow (NEON), else two. static constexpr idx mr = std::min<idx>(14, ((- b_vectors - 2) / b_vectors) & ~idx{1}) Rows of the register tile: what remains of the file after the B vectors and two broadcast registers, at most 14, rounded to even. static constexpr idx nr = b_vectors * width Columns of the register tile. static constexpr idx kc = std::clamp<idx>(detail::round_down((/ 2) / (sizeof(T) * nr), 8), 8, 512) Inner-product length per microkernel call: the kc x nr B sliver takes half of L1. Capped at 512, since a longer kc only shrinks the other blocks. static constexpr idx mc = std::max<idx>( mr, detail::round_down(std::min<idx>(/ 2, idx{1} << 20) / (sizeof(T) * kc), mr)) Rows of the packed A slab: half of L2, at most 1 MiB. static constexpr idx nc = std::max<idx>(nr, detail::round_down(/ (sizeof(T) * kc), nr)) Columns of the packed B panel. static constexpr idx workspace = (mc * kc) + (kc * nc) Elements of workspace the packed panels need at their largest.

docs.title: num::kernel::hessenberg_shifted_factor
docs.text:
Defined in header <kernel/complex.hpp>

template <std::floating_point T, class Index>
void hessenberg_shifted_factor(std::complex<T> *work, const T *H, std::complex<T> shift,
                               idx n, Index *piv) noexcept;

Factor \(sI - H\) in place for an upper Hessenberg \(H\), in \(O(n^2)\).

Only one subdiagonal entry per column is eliminated, and pivoting compares it against the diagonal. This makes each shift of a Krylov resolvent cheap.

  • H: Upper Hessenberg matrix, n*n row-major, real.
  • shift: Complex shift \(s\).
  • n: Dimension.
  • piv: Output pivot record, length n.

docs.title: num::kernel::householder_vector
docs.text:
Defined in header <kernel/rotations.hpp>

template <std::floating_point T>
void householder_vector(T *v, T &beta, const T *x, idx m) noexcept;

Computes elementary Householder reflector vector \(\mathbf{v}\) and scalar \(\beta\) such that:

\[ (I - \beta \mathbf{v} \mathbf{v}^T) \mathbf{x} = \mp \|\mathbf{x}\|_2 \mathbf{e}_1 \]

\(\mathbf{v}\) is sized \(m\), with \(v_0 = 1\) implicitly assigned.

docs.title: num::kernel::householder_vector_strided
docs.text:
Defined in header <kernel/rotations.hpp>

template <std::floating_point T>
void householder_vector_strided(T *v, T &beta, const T *A, idx lda, idx offset,
                                idx m) noexcept;

Householder reflector for a strided column of a matrix.

The column is copied into v and the reflector formed there in place. Not a call to householder_vector(v, beta, v, m): that passes one buffer as two restrict parameters, and at -O3 the compiler is entitled to read x[0] after v[0] has been overwritten with 1.

docs.title: num::kernel::ilu0_factor
docs.text:
Defined in header <kernel/sparse.hpp>

template <std::floating_point T, std::integral Index>
bool ilu0_factor(T *val, const Index *row_ptr, const Index *col_idx,
                 const Index *diagonal, Index *scratch,
                 std::type_identity_t<Index> n) noexcept;

In-place ILU(0) factorization of a CSR value array.

scratch maps columns to positions in the row being eliminated, so matching a pivot row's column is O(1). It is cleared on exit from each row.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• val: CSR values, overwritten with the combined factors.
  • row_ptr: CSR row offsets, size n+1. Not modified.
  • col_idx: CSR column indices, sorted within each row. Not modified.
  • diagonal: Diagonal positions from csr_diagonal_positions.
  • scratch: Workspace of size n; contents on entry and exit are irrelevant.
  • n: Number of rows.

docs.title: Return value
docs.text: False if a pivot was zero or non-finite, leaving val partially overwritten.

docs.text:
Defined in header <kernel/factor.hpp>

template <std::floating_point T, class Index>
void lu_invert(T *inverse, const T *LU, const Index *piv, idx n, T *work) noexcept;

Inverse from packed LU factors: inverse <- A^{-1}, one column at a time.

Column j of the inverse is the solve A x = e_j, so this is n calls of lu_solve written without the per-column copy. Out of place: every column's solve reads the whole factor, so the result cannot overwrite it. work holds n elements.

Defined in header <kernel/rotations.hpp>

void qr_apply_block_left(T *C, idx ldc, idx rows, idx cols, const T *V, const T *Tm,
                         idx kb, bool transpose, T *W) noexcept;

C <- (I - V T' V^T) C for a compact-WY block reflector.

C is rows x cols; V and T come from qr_form_block with kb reflectors; T' is T^T when transpose is set (the product \(H_{k_b-1} \cdots H_0\), used when factoring) and T otherwise (\(H_0 \cdots H_{k_b-1}\), used when forming Q). W holds kb x cols.

void qr_form_block(T *V, T *Tm, const T *A, idx lda, idx m, idx k0, idx kb,
                   const T *tau) noexcept;

Form the compact-WY block reflector for columns [k0, k0 + kb).

Reads the reflector tails stored below the diagonal of the factored panel and their scalars tau, and writes V ((m - k0) x kb, unit lower trapezoidal, row stride kb) and the upper triangular T (kb x kb) with \(H_{k_0} \cdots H_{k_0 + k_b - 1} = I - V T V^T\).

Defined in header <kernel/dense.hpp>

Solves L*X=B in-place for row-major X with nrhs columns.

Blocked by detail::trsm_block rows of the triangle: each diagonal block is a short substitution, and the rows beneath it are updated by gemm, so for n past one block the work runs at gemm speed. Vectorization within a block is across the independent right-hand sides.

                                        idx n) noexcept;

Solves X*L^T=B in-place for row-major panel rows.

X is rows x n, L is lower triangular n x n; each row is an independent right-side solve. This is the panel solve in blocked Cholesky: L21 <- A21 * L11^{-T}. Blocked by columns of X: after a diagonal block is solved, the columns to its right are updated by gemm.

docs.title: num::ode::debug::verify_order_of_accuracy
docs.text:
Defined in header <ode/debug.hpp>

template <class Advance>
void verify_order_of_accuracy(
    Advance &&advance, const vec &y0, real t0, real t1, real claimed_order,
    real slack = 0.4, std::source_location loc = std::source_location::current());

Measure the observed order of accuracy of a one-step integrator.

Integrates with steps \(h\) and \(h/2\) against a reference at \(h/16\). The error ratio approaches \(2^p\), so its \(\log_2\) recovers \(p\).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• advance: Callable (real t0, real t1, real h, const vec &y0, vec &y1).
  • y0: Initial state.
  • t0: Start of the integration interval.
  • t1: End of the integration interval.
  • claimed_order: The order the method advertises.
  • slack: Tolerated shortfall in the measured order.
  • loc: Call site reported in the diagnostic.

docs.title: num::ode::debug::verify_symplectic_2form
docs.text:
Defined in header <ode/debug.hpp>

template <class Step>
void verify_symplectic_2form(
    Step &&step, const vec &q0, const vec &p0, real h, real tol = 1e-6,
    std::source_location loc = std::source_location::current());

Verify that one step preserves the symplectic 2-form \(\omega = dq \wedge dp\).

Two tangent vectors are propagated by finite differences, and their pairing \(\omega(u,v) = \delta q_u \cdot \delta p_v - \delta q_v \cdot \delta p_u\) must be unchanged.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• step: Callable (const vec &q, const vec &p, real h, vec &q1, vec &p1).
  • q0: Position at which to test.
  • p0: Momentum at which to test.
  • h: Step size.
  • tol: Relative tolerance on the preserved form.
  • loc: Call site reported in the diagnostic.

docs.title: num::operators::restricted_laws
docs.text:
Defined in header <operator/projected.hpp>

template <class Op, class Subspace>
using restricted_laws = std::conditional_t<
    claims<Op, law::spd>, law::list<law::spd_on<Subspace>>,
    std::conditional_t<
        claims<Op, law::psd>, law::list<law::psd_on<Subspace>>,
        std::conditional_t<claims<Op, law::self_adjoint>,
                           law::list<law::self_adjoint_on<Subspace>>, law::list<>>>>;

The law of \(P_S A\) on S for an operator A claiming a self-adjoint law.

\(P_S A\) is not self-adjoint even when A is, but \(P_S A x = P_S A P_S x\) for \(x \in S\), and \(P_S A P_S\) keeps A's law on S. This lets num::pcg solve with a graph Laplacian on the zero-sum subspace without a second assertion.

docs.text:
Defined in header <spatial/debug.hpp>

template <class K, class Scalar = float>
requires smoothing_kernel<K, Scalar>
void verify_kernel_normalization(
    Scalar h, Scalar tol = Scalar(2e-2),
    std::source_location loc = std::source_location::current());

Verify that a smoothing kernel integrates to one over its support.

\[ \int_0^{2h} W(r,h) \, 2\pi r \, dr = 1 \]

SPH interpolates a field as \(\sum_j m_j (\rho_j)^{-1} A_j W_{ij}\), which reproduces a constant only when the kernel is normalized. A kernel that is not produces densities off by a constant factor, which looks like a physical result rather than an error.

docs.title: num::spectral::dst1
docs.text:
Defined in header <spectral/dst.hpp>

vec dst1(const vec &x);

Unnormalised DST-I of an N-point vector via complex FFT.

X[k] = sum_{j=1}^{N} x[j] * sin(jkpi/(N+1)), k = 1..N (stored 0-indexed). Odd-extension y = [0, x, 0, -rev(x)] has length M = 2(N+1). FFT(y)[k] = -2i * sum sin(...) => DST(x)[k-1] = -Im(FFT(y)[k]) / 2.

Verify Parseval's identity for a forward transform.

\[ \sum_n |x_n|^2 = \frac{1}{N} \sum_k |X_k|^2 \]

A transform that violates it is not unitary after normalization, and a spectral method built on it will gain or lose energy every step.

docs.title: num::structures::sample_biclique_tree
docs.text:
Defined in header <structures/graph/clique.hpp>

template <typename Weight, typename Rng, typename Emit>
void sample_biclique_tree(const array<Weight> &x, const array<Weight> &y, Weight pivot,
                          Rng &rng, std::size_t trees, Emit emit);

Sample a spanning tree of the directed product biclique left by an LU pivot.

Eliminating pivot v leaves the rank-one Schur update \(xy^{T}/a\), with \(x_i = -A_{iv}\), \(y_j = -A_{vj}\) and \(a = A_{vv}\). Each in-neighbour becomes \(i_L\) and each out-neighbour \(j_R\) of a bipartite graph with conductances \(x_iy_j/a\). Edge \(i_L j_R\) enters the tree with probability \(p_{ij} = 1 - (1-\alpha_i)(1-\beta_j)\), where \(\alpha_i = x_i/X\) and \(\beta_j = y_j/Y\), and reweighting by \(w_{ij}/p_{ij}\) gives \(\mathbb{E}[\widetilde S_v] = xy^{T}/a\). It requires \(x_i, y_j, a > 0\), as in a nonsymmetric M-matrix; otherwise nothing is emitted. The derivation is in the algorithm notes.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• x: Incoming conductances, all strictly positive.
  • y: Outgoing conductances, all strictly positive.
  • pivot: \(a = A_{vv}\), strictly positive.
  • rng: Random source.
  • trees: Independent trees to average; each sampled weight is divided by this.
  • emit: Callable void(std::size_t i, std::size_t j, Weight w) receiving directed fill.

docs.title: num::structures::sample_clique_tree
docs.text:
Defined in header <structures/graph/clique.hpp>

template <typename Weight, std::integral Index, typename Queue, typename Rng>
void sample_clique_tree(array<array<multi_edge<Weight, Index>>> &G, Queue &q,
                        const array<multi_edge<Weight, Index>> &nbr,
                        Weight total_weight, Rng &rng, std::size_t trees = 1);

Replace the star-mesh clique by a random spanning tree of it, reweighted so the elimination stays unbiased in expectation.

Eliminating v adds a clique on its neighbours with weights \(w_{ij} = c_i c_j / C\), where \(c_i\) is the conductance from v to i and \(C = \sum_i c_i\). Edge \(ij\) enters the tree with probability \(p_{ij} = (c_i + c_j)/C\) and is reweighted to the harmonic mean \(c_i c_j / (c_i + c_j)\), so \(\mathbb{E}[\widetilde L^{(v)}] = \mathrm{Sc}(L)\). The walk is capped: past the cap the remaining vertices attach to the heaviest neighbour, which keeps a spanning tree but loses exactness for that elimination. The derivation and measured behaviour are in the algorithm notes.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• G: Adjacency being eliminated; sampled edges are appended.
  • q: Degree queue, rekeyed for each endpoint touched.
  • nbr: Neighbours of the eliminated vertex, with their conductances.
  • total_weight: \(C\), the sum of those conductances.
  • rng: Random source.

Sample the equivalence-relation axioms a union-find claims: reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity, and connected(u,v) agreeing with \(\mathrm{find}(u) = \mathrm{find}(v)\). Takes a mutable reference because path compression rewrites the forest.

docs.title: num::unsafe::cg
docs.text:
Defined in header <linear/solvers/cg.hpp>

solver_result cg(const mat &A, const vec &b, vec &x, cg_options options = {});

Conjugate gradients on a stored matrix, without requiring the SPD invariant.

On an indefinite or non-symmetric matrix the iteration breaks down silently. Runs through num::accel; num::unsafe::cuda::cg works on device buffers.

docs.title: Return value
docs.text: solver_result: .iterations, .residual (final residual norm), .converged.

docs.title: num::unsafe::cholesky
docs.text:
Defined in header <linear/factorization/cholesky.hpp>

cholesky_result cholesky(const mat &A);

Factor \(A = LL^T\) without requiring or checking the SPD invariant.

The deliberate escape hatch. Calling this says, at the call site and in a form that survives grep, that the SPD precondition is being taken on faith. Nothing is sampled; if A is not positive definite the factorization simply reports failure through cholesky_result::success.

docs.title: num::unsafe::eig_sym
docs.text:
Defined in header <linear/eigen/jacobi_eig.hpp>

eigen_result eig_sym(const mat &A, real tol = 1e-12, idx max_sweeps = 100);

Symmetric eigendecomposition without requiring or checking the symmetry invariant.

Reads only the lower triangle, so an asymmetric matrix yields the spectrum of its symmetric part rather than an error.

docs.title: num::unsafe::lanczos
docs.text:
Defined in header <linear/eigen/lanczos.hpp>

lanczos_result lanczos(const mat &A, idx k, real tol = 1e-10, idx max_steps = 0);  // (1)

lanczos_result lanczos(const spmat &A, idx k, real tol = 1e-10, idx max_steps = 0);  // (2)

(1) Lanczos on a stored dense matrix without requiring the symmetry invariant.

The three-term recurrence is derived from \(A = A^T\); without it the basis loses orthogonality and the Ritz values are not eigenvalue estimates.

(2) Lanczos on a stored sparse matrix without requiring the symmetry invariant.
